questions.q: What is the type of a?
questions.explain: The candidate for T is the literal "NGN". T is the whole return type, so the literal is kept, and a const does not widen it.

questions.q: What is the type of c?
questions.explain: When T only appears inside something (a property, an array), the inferred literal is widened to string, because the container usually holds other values later.

questions.q: Which change makes boxed("NGN") return { value: "NGN" } without the caller writing anything extra?
questions.explain: A constraint that mentions a primitive type tells TypeScript the exact value matters, so the literal is kept even inside the object. A const type parameter would also work.
options: Adding a return type annotation : { value: string }
Constraining the type parameter: <T extends string>

questions.q: What is the type of b?
questions.explain: T is inferred as "NGN", but a let may be reassigned, so the variable's type is widened, exactly as for let b = "NGN".

questions.q: What does the compiler say about this call?
questions.explain: With competing candidates and no common supertype among them, the first candidate wins and the other argument is reported. That catches "same type" arguments that are not the same type. Write pair<number | string>(…) or use two type parameters if mixing is intended.
options: TS2345 on "NGN": T was inferred as number from the first argument

questions.q: What is a context-sensitive argument?
questions.explain: TypeScript infers type parameters from the other arguments first, then checks the context-sensitive callbacks with those types. That is how (input) => … can get a type that comes from another argument.
options: An argument that depends on a runtime condition
An expression, such as an arrow function with unannotated parameters, whose type needs a contextual type; TypeScript checks it after the other arguments
An argument whose value is a literal
Any argument to a generic function

questions.q: Why does the second call report 'input' is of type 'unknown'?
questions.explain: Context-sensitive functions in an object literal are inferred left to right. Put the property that produces a type before the one that consumes it, or annotate the consumer's parameter.
options: Because run must always be declared last in an interface
Because properties are processed in order: run is checked before parse has produced a candidate for In
Because object literals cannot contain two callbacks

questions.q: Which of these does not give an arrow function's parameters a contextual type?
questions.explain: A contextual type flows into an expression from the place it is written. A later use of the variable does not flow back, so the parameters are implicitly any (TS7006).
options: Passing it directly as an argument to a function that declares the callback type
Writing it in an object literal followed by satisfies Record<string, (id: string) => void>
Assigning it to a variable annotated with a function type
Declaring it in its own const and passing that variable to the function later

questions.q: Why does a recursive function without a return type annotation report TS7023?
questions.explain: The inference is circular, so TypeScript gives up and would use any, which strict mode reports. A return type annotation breaks the circle.
options: Because recursion is not allowed in strict mode
Because inferring its return type requires the type of its own recursive call, which is the type being inferred
Because recursive functions must be declared with function
Because the call stack may overflow

questions.q: In function applyVat(order) { return order.totalKobo * 1.075; }, what type does TypeScript infer for order?
questions.explain: TypeScript never infers parameter types from the function body. Parameters are the boundary where you declare what the function accepts.
options: { totalKobo: number }, from how the body uses it
None: without an annotation or a context it is implicitly any, which strict mode reports as TS7006

questions.q: What is the type of x?
questions.explain: A const type parameter infers as if the caller had written as const: literals kept, arrays become readonly tuples, properties become read-only.

questions.q: What is the type of fromVariable?
questions.explain: const T only affects literals written in the call. roles was already widened to string[] when it was declared, and the call cannot bring the literals back.

questions.q: Which mistake does as const catch in const METHODS = ["GET", "POST", "GTE"] as const;?
questions.explain: A const assertion preserves; it has no target type to check against. Add satisfies readonly Method[] to check the values.
options: None; as const keeps values precise and read-only, but checks nothing about them
That the array should be frozen

questions.q: What does as const change in the JavaScript that runs?
questions.explain: readonly exists only for the compiler. Use Object.freeze when the value must really not change at runtime.
options: It makes the value a constant in the engine
Nothing; it is erased, and the object can still be changed by code the compiler does not stop

questions.q: Which line is a compile error?
questions.explain: A const assertion can only be applied to literals (and enum member references): TS1355. A function call's result already has its type; there is no literal to keep.

questions.q: What is the type of r.method?
questions.explain: satisfies gives the literal a contextual type. Where that type contains literal types, the literal is checked against them and kept, so method is "GET" without as const. The variable keeps its own type, not Method.
questions.code:
type Method = "GET" | "POST";
const r = { method: "GET", path: "/products" } satisfies { method: Method; path: string };

questions.q: What is the type of r.method now?
questions.explain: The contextual type for method is string, which has no literal types in it, so the literal is widened as usual.
questions.code: const r = { method: "GET", path: "/products" } satisfies { method: string; path: string };

questions.q: What is the type of orderId inside refund?
questions.explain: satisfies contextually types the whole literal, including the callbacks inside it. With as const alone there would be no context and orderId would be an implicit any.

questions.q: Which line compiles and produces a checked, read-only tuple readonly ["NGN", "USD"]?
questions.explain: as const must be applied to the literal itself, then satisfies checks the result. The annotated version checks too, but its type is the general readonly Currency[], and as checks almost nothing.
options: const c = ["NGN", "USD"] satisfies readonly Currency[] as const;
const c = ["NGN", "USD"] as const satisfies readonly Currency[];

questions.q: const routes: Record<string, RouteDef> = { listProducts: { … } }; What happens with routes.listProdcts.handler?
questions.explain: An annotation replaces the value's type with the annotated one, and that type has an index signature. The typo is only caught with satisfies, which keeps the exact keys.
options: A compile error: property does not exist
It compiles, because every string is a valid key of Record<string, RouteDef>, and it throws at runtime

questions.q: An array of routes, one of them missing its handler, ends in as RouteDef[] and compiles. Why?
questions.explain: An assertion rejects only conversions between types that do not overlap at all. Whether an incomplete entry is caught depends on the other entries and on literal types, so it is not a check you can rely on.
options: Because an assertion only requires the types to overlap, and the element type is a union that includes a complete route, which overlaps with RouteDef

questions.q: When is an annotation better than satisfies for a value you write?
questions.explain: satisfies keeps details you may not want to commit to. let current: Route = routes.home must accept other routes later, and a public export's type is a promise to its users.
options: When you want the variable to have exactly the general type, for example because it will be reassigned, or because it is exported and callers should not depend on its details

questions.q: What is Role?
questions.explain: typeof ROLES is the readonly tuple, and indexing it with number gives the type of any element: the union. Without as const it would be string.
questions.code:
const ROLES = ["public", "customer", "admin"] as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];

questions.q: What does AdminRoute compute?
questions.explain: The mapped type gives each route either its own name or never. Indexing it with all its keys collects the values into a union, and the nevers disappear. It only works because satisfies kept each route's literal auth.
questions.code: type AdminRoute = { [N in RouteName]: (typeof routes)[N]["auth"] extends "admin" ? N : never }[RouteName];
options: An object with one property per admin route
The union of the route names whose auth is "admin"
The handlers of the admin routes

questions.q: During a refactor, someone replaces satisfies Record<string, RouteDef> with an annotation. Which test notices?
questions.explain: The runtime behaviour does not change, so runtime tests pass. The inferred types do change, silently switching off checks in code like link. Type tests pin the inferred facts you depend on.
options: None; the code still compiles and runs
A type test such as Expect<Equal<RouteName, "listProducts" | "getOrder" | "refundOrder">>, because RouteName becomes string

options:
/products 2 products
/orders TypeError: route.handler is not a function
TypeError: route.handler is not a function

questions.explain: The let widened to string, so the reassignment is allowed. At runtime, typeof reports JavaScript's type, which is always "string"; literal types exist only in the compiler.

questions.explain: Object.freeze really prevents changes. Module code runs in strict mode, where writing to a frozen property throws a TypeError instead of failing silently.

questions.explain: With the annotation, any string key is allowed at compile time, so only runtime code can notice the typo. Here ?. and ?? handle it; without them, reading .handler would throw.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'handler')

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: satisfies changes nothing at runtime. It checked both entries, and it kept the precise type, so fees.NGN.capKobo is known to be a number without !.

questions.explain: Each :name is replaced by its encoded value. Encoding turns the space and the / into escapes, so a value can never add path segments or change the route.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A customer ranks above public and below admin. ROLES still exists at runtime, so it can be searched; the Role type was derived from it.

questions.explain: parse comes first, so In is inferred as { orderId: string; attempts: number } before run is checked. trim() removes the spaces and the attempt count is a number, so + 1 adds.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: One product at the top, two in Shoes, none in Bags itself and one in Wallets: 4. The return type annotation is what lets this recursive function compile.

questions.q: pair uses one type parameter for both arguments, so pair(150_000, "NGN") does not compile. Rewrite it with two type parameters, returning a tuple of both. The program should print [ 150000, 'NGN' ] [ 'ORD-7', true ].
questions.explain: Each type parameter now gets one candidate from its own argument, so nothing competes. The result type is [number, string] for the first call.

questions.q: Write defineRoutes, a helper that checks a table against Record<string, RouteDef> and returns it unchanged with its precise type (use a const type parameter). The program should print order ORD-9 GET.
questions.explain: The constraint checks the table and gives params its type; const T keeps the literal method and path. It is the function form of as const satisfies.

questions.q: Finish isRole, a type guard backed by the ROLES list, and use it to keep only valid roles from a list loaded from a database. The program should print [ 'customer', 'admin' ].
questions.explain: The union type and the runtime list come from the same as const array, so they cannot drift. The comparison is exact: "Admin" is not a role.

questions.q: Finish the recursive totalKobo(category): the sum of the prices in a category and all its sub-categories. Give it a return type annotation (it is required for recursion). The program should print 3250000.
questions.explain: Without : number, TypeScript would need the function's own return type to infer it, and would report TS7023. The base case is a category with no children: the second reduce returns 0.

questions.q: Finish link(path, params): replace every :name in the path with the URL-encoded value of params[name]. The program should print /shops/ada%20stores/orders/ORD-9.
questions.explain: A replace callback receives each captured name. Encoding every value keeps spaces and slashes from breaking the URL. The lesson's typed link adds a compile-time check that the params object has exactly the path's parameter names.

questions.q: Replace the as Settings with as const satisfies Settings and fix the value the check then reports, so the program prints NGN card,transfer 7.5.
questions.explain: The double assertion hid a VAT written as text, which crashes at toFixed. satisfies reports it at compile time, and as const keeps the exact values.
